title: Under-scalp electrodes barely sharpen EEG maps of cortex while electrodes in or below the bone do, in layered head models checked on 61 recordings of known intracerebral sources
abstract: Electrodes placed under the scalp, on the skull, show cortical activity almost as blurred as scalp electrodes; electrodes must go into or below the bone, and be closely spaced, to give much sharper maps. This matters because minimally invasive EEG implants under the scalp and very dense scalp caps are now in use, and both are often expected to improve spatial detail. We calculated the potential of cortical current sources in layered spherical head models (brain, cerebrospinal fluid, skull, scalp) at five electrode depths, and how finely an electrode array can separate independent cortical patches when electrode noise is present (optimal linear estimate; checked against an exact matrix calculation within 17 percent). We tested the model with a public data set (Localize-MI) in which known currents were injected inside the brains of 7 patients while 256 scalp electrodes recorded (61 recordings). The model correlated with the measured scalp maps at a median of 0.91 and fitted the distance dependence of spontaneous EEG, which set the single-trial noise level. A 10 nAm dipole 1.5 mm below the brain surface gives a half-maximum radius of 29 mm on the scalp, 23 mm under the scalp, 6 mm inside the bone and 3 mm on the dura. For single trials, arrays under the scalp resolve cortical patches only 1.04 to 1.20 times smaller than scalp arrays of equal 5 mm spacing (12 head-model variants); arrays inside or below the bone resolve patches 2.3 to 5.0 times smaller (about 5 mm), but dural arrays with 10 mm or wider spacing leave most of the cortex between electrodes unseen. A scalp cap with 8.6 mm spacing instead of 15.7 mm makes the resolvable patch 1.12 to 1.26 times smaller. The measured maps also hold a reproducible fine structure that a smooth head model does not produce: interpolation from the other electrodes misses 20 percent of the map amplitude, mostly at a few electrodes, and the structure is mostly specific to the stimulated electrode shaft, with a small position-like part per electrode. If an error of 8 to 16 percent per electrode remains in averaged scalp EEG, halving it helps about as much as 3.3 times more channels. Limits: spherical geometry, a radial source sheet, assumed implant noise, no muscle artefacts, and one patient data set with skull openings.
